tricks.original_title: Set Tuning to Equal Temperament unless you mean otherwise
tricks.reason: Apple says the Tuning settings control the real-time tuning system used with Logic's INCLUDED software instruments, so 'every software instrument' overreaches. Also, Apple names the option 'Equal Tempered' and documents the Tune slider (default A 440 Hz).
tricks.final_title: Check Tuning when a synth sounds subtly off
tricks.final_body: Project Settings > Tuning sets the tuning for Logic's included software instruments. If a synth sounds subtly wrong against a sample, check here first: Equal Tempered turns off any alternative tuning, and the Tune slider should read A 440 Hz unless you meant to change it.

sources.label: Apple - Tuning project settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Tuning settings change the real-time tuning system used with the included software instruments; Equal Tempered turns off any tuning and uses an equal tempered scale; the Tune slider sets global tuning, default concert pitch A (440 Hz).

tricks.original_title: Turn on “Bounce project settings” for consistent exports
tricks.reason: The 'Bounce project settings' title names something that does not exist. The body contained an editorial 'Retitle to' note. Apple supports the Assets path, the 'Copy audio files into project' checkbox, files being copied on the next save, and being able to move or copy the project afterwards. The specific list (Ultrabeat, Sampler, Space Designer IRs, Sound Library content) was not confirmed for the current Assets pane, so it was generalised.
tricks.final_title: Copy your assets into the project so it travels
tricks.final_body: In File > Project Settings > Assets, select the copy checkboxes, such as "Copy audio files into project". The files are copied in the next time you save. From then on you can move or copy the project without losing any file references.

sources.label: Apple - Manage project assets in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Choose File > Project Settings > Assets; select any of the copy checkboxes ('Copy audio files into project' stores all audio files in the project package or folder); files are copied when the project is saved; afterwards you can move or copy the project without losing references.

tricks.original_title: Save a Session Start template and set it as the default
tricks.reason: Apple documents File > Save As Template. It also documents a Startup Action pop-up with 'Create New Project Using Default Template' and a Default Template button that picks the template to open.
tricks.final_title: Save a Session Start template and set it as the default
tricks.final_body: Build one project with your usual tracks, buses, reverb and marker colours, then File > Save as Template. Set it to open on launch and you never build a session from zero again.

sources.label: Apple - Project Handling settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Startup Action pop-up includes 'Create New Project Using Default Template'; the Default Template button chooses that template; File > Save As Template saves a template, found under My Templates in the Project Chooser.

tricks.original_title: Set a default channel strip for new tracks
tricks.reason: Apple supports saving through Setting button > 'Save Channel Strip Setting as' and loading settings from the Setting button pop-up or the Library. No source was found for the 'User Channel Strip Settings' folder name or the 'every new track is two clicks' claim, and there is no documented 'default channel strip' feature. The title now describes what Apple actually documents.
tricks.final_title: Save your starting channel strip as a setting
tricks.final_body: Build one channel strip the way you always start: your go-to EQ, compressor and sends. Click the Setting button at the top of the strip, choose "Save Channel Strip Setting as", pick a folder, name it and click Save. On any new track, load it from the Setting button's pop-up menu or from the Library.

sources.label: Apple - Work with channel strip settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Click the Setting button, choose 'Save Channel Strip Setting as', select a folder, name it, click Save; load settings from the Setting button pop-up menu, or click the triangle beside the Setting button so the Library shows channel strip settings.

tricks.original_title: Set the default region colour palette
tricks.reason: There is no source for a persistent 'default region colour palette' (Apple's Colors project settings cover Score pitch, velocity and user colours, not regions). Apple supports Option-C and Name and Color > Show/Hide Colors. The custom-colour step was dropped because the current result wording ('click any color') conflicts with the prior 'double-click'. The part about building the scheme into a template is workflow advice.
tricks.final_title: Give each colour a fixed meaning
tricks.final_body: Press ⌥C to open the Color palette (or Control-click a region and choose Name and Color > Show/Hide Colors), then click a colour. Decide once what each colour means to you (drums, vocals, keys, reference) and colour your template that way, so every project opens with the same language.

sources.label: Apple - Color regions in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Control-click a selected region, choose Name and Color > Show/Hide Colors (or press Option-C), then click a color.

tricks.original_title: Turn on Project Alternatives before you need them
tricks.reason: The menu paths, Done, Edit Alternatives, and the fact that you cannot remove Main are all confirmed by Apple. Apple's Advanced settings page confirms project alternatives need Enable Complete Features (Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced). The title implied Alternatives is a switch you turn on, so it was retitled, and the settings path was made exact.
tricks.final_title: Make a Project Alternative before big changes
tricks.final_body: File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative gives you another version of the project: name it and click Done. Make one before every big arrangement change. Alternatives need Enable Complete Features in Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced. File > Project Alternatives > Edit Alternatives lets you rename or delete them; you can't remove the Main alternative.

sources.label: Apple - Use project alternatives and backups in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative, enter a unique name, click Done; File > Project Alternatives > Edit Alternatives to rename or delete; you cannot remove the Main alternative.

sources.label: Apple - Advanced settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: With Enable Complete Features selected (Logic Pro > Settings > Advanced), advanced features such as project alternatives and backups are available.

tricks.original_title: Set autosave and then still hit ⌘S
tricks.reason: The body contained an editorial 'Retitle to' note. The claim 'there is no autosave setting' is supported only by forum posts (logicprohelp, Apple Community), which is below the bar, so it was dropped. Apple fully supports the backup behaviour: each File > Save / Command-S saves a backup, up to ten per alternative, listed newest first under File > Revert to. Backups need Complete Features.
tricks.final_title: Hit ⌘S often: every save banks a backup
tricks.final_body: Each time you save with File > Save (⌘S), Logic keeps a backup of the current project alternative, up to ten per alternative. To go back, choose File > Revert to and pick one; they're listed newest first. Backups need Enable Complete Features. Build the reflex of hitting ⌘S every time you finish a thought.

sources.label: Apple - Use project alternatives and backups in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Each time you save using File > Save (or Command-S), a version of the current project alternative is saved (up to ten backups per alternative); File > Revert to lists backups newest to oldest.

sources.label: Apple - Advanced settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Enable Complete Features makes project alternatives and backups available.

tricks.original_title: Move the Sound Library to an external drive on purpose
tricks.reason: Not re-searched (budget); not rewritten. The prior audit's Apple KB quote supports the exact menu path. 'Tens of gigabytes' and 'without breaking a single patch' are unsupported. tricks.final_title: Move the Sound Library to an external drive on purpose
tricks.final_body: Logic Pro > Sound Library > Relocate Sound Library moves the library off your system drive: pick the drive or volume and click Relocate. Afterwards, don't rename that drive, or Logic Pro won't be able to find the Sound Library.

sources.evidence: Prior audit quote: choose Logic Pro > Sound Library > Relocate Sound Library, select the storage device or volume, click Relocate; don't rename the device afterwards or Logic Pro and MainStage won't find the Sound Library.

tricks.final_title: Save the project as a Package so it travels
tricks.final_body: In the File > Save As dialog, choose "Organize my project as: Package" and select the asset types to copy into it. Assets saved in the project are still there when you move or copy it. Choose Folder instead if you want a project folder with subfolders for each asset type.

sources.evidence: 'Organize my project as: Package' saves a file (package) containing project assets; 'Organize my project as: Folder' saves a folder with subfolders for assets; select asset types to copy; saving assets in the project keeps them available when you move or copy it.

tricks.final_title: Drag one arrangement marker onto another to swap sections

tricks.original_title: ⌥‑drag an arrangement marker to duplicate a section
tricks.reason: The current Apple Edit arrangement markers page gives Option-drag as the way to copy a marker, and says a copy brings along all regions and automation in the section. This was re-confirmed by a search that returned the page.
tricks.final_title: ⌥‑drag an arrangement marker to duplicate a section
tricks.final_body: Hold ⌥ and drag any arrangement marker to copy that entire section, contents and all, to a new point in the timeline.

sources.label: Apple — Edit arrangement markers in Logic Pro for Mac

tricks.original_title: Delete a section and close the gap

tricks.final_body: Select the arrangement marker and press Delete once — that removes the section's regions. Press Delete again and the marker goes too, pulling everything after it back to close the hole.

sources.label: Apple — Edit arrangement markers in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Select the arrangement marker, then press Delete to delete the regions below it so it is empty. Press Delete again to delete the arrangement marker. Sections to the right move left to fill the deleted section.

tricks.original_title: Insert silence across the whole project
tricks.reason: macProVideo, 9to5Mac and Apple's /10.7/ Add or remove gaps page all agree on the menu path Edit > Cut/Insert Time > Insert Silence Between Locators. The behaviour described now (regions split at the left locator and moved past the right locator) is supported.
tricks.final_title: Insert silence across the whole project
tricks.final_body: Set the locators around the gap you want, then choose Edit > Cut/Insert Time > Insert Silence Between Locators. Regions are cut at the left locator and everything after it moves past the right locator — the quick way to add two bars to an intro.

sources.label: macProVideo — Making Whole Project Edits in Logic Pro
sources.evidence: Insert Silence Between Locators is accessed via Edit > Cut/Insert Time; regions longer than the cycle are cut at the left locator and the second part moved to the right of the right locator.

sources.evidence: Insert Silence creates a gap anywhere in the arrangement, useful to bump the whole song over to make room for an intro; set it up with a left/right locator selection.

sources.label: Apple — Add or remove gaps in Logic Pro (10.7 page)
sources.evidence: Choose Edit > Cut/Insert Time > Insert Silence Between Locators; if no selection is made, all regions between the locators are affected.

tricks.original_title: Snap arrangement markers to your actual section boundaries
tricks.reason: Apple confirms that new markers appear at the project start or after the last marker, eight bars long, regardless of playhead position, and that you resize them by dragging the right edge. No source mentions the locators or says the edge 'snaps to bars', so both were removed. The key U has nothing to do with this trick and was removed.
tricks.final_title: Resize arrangement markers to fit your sections
tricks.final_body: New arrangement markers always appear at the start of the project or after the last existing marker, eight bars long, regardless of the playhead position. So create the marker first, then drag its right edge left or right until it matches the section.

sources.label: Apple — Add arrangement markers in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The arrangement marker appears at the start of the project or at the end of the last existing arrangement marker, regardless of the playhead position; it is eight bars long; drag the right edge left or right to resize it.

The book says Play from Selection defaults to ⇧Space, but Apple's Control playback page gives the key as Shift-Return, and that page exists only with /10.7/ in the URL. No current Apple page settled the default key, and the 'several selection-based playback commands' claim was never sourced. Without a trustworthy key, the tip has nothing left.

sources.label: Apple — Control playback in Logic Pro (10.7-versioned page)
sources.evidence: The Play from Selection button plays from the start point of the first selected region or event, and the key command given is Shift-Return, not Shift-Space.

tricks.original_title: Scroll horizontally without the scrollbar
tricks.reason: The 'drag two fingers to scroll horizontally and vertically' quote comes from Apple's iPad guide, not the Mac guide. Apple's current Mac page only says a gesture-capable trackpad can scroll and zoom the Tracks area, and that you can swipe on the Touch Bar to scroll. The rewrite keeps only those claims.
tricks.final_title: Scroll without the scrollbar
tricks.final_body: If your Mac has a trackpad that supports gestures, you can scroll and zoom the Tracks area with gestures instead of reaching for the scrollbars. On a Mac with a Touch Bar, swipe left or right on the Touch Bar to scroll through the visible area of the project.

sources.label: Apple — Scroll and zoom in the Tracks area in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: If your computer has a trackpad that supports gestures, you can also scroll and zoom the Tracks area using gestures. On Macs with a Touch Bar, swipe left or right on the Touch Bar to scroll through the visible area of the project.

tricks.original_title: Use the Cycle area as a bookmark
tricks.reason: U is 'Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events and Enable Cycle': it rounds the locators to the nearest bar lines around the selection and turns Cycle on. ⌘U is 'Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop', with no rounding. Apple describes the cycle area as a yellow strip in the ruler. No current, unversioned Apple cycle-area page came up. The key commands rest on studio-interns and afteraudio's Global Commands listing, and 'yellow strip' only on the /10.7/ Apple page.
tricks.final_title: Use the Cycle area as a bookmark
tricks.final_body: Select the region or passage you are working on and press U. Logic sets the left and right locators around it — rounded to bar lines — and turns Cycle on, so the yellow strip in the ruler marks your work area and keeps looping it. Use ⌘U instead if you want the locators exactly on the selection boundaries rather than rounded.

sources.label: studio-interns.com — Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events (keyboard command of the day)
sources.evidence: Documents the Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events command. The search summary says the command rounds the locators to the bar lines nearest the start and end of the selection, and it gives the key as U.

sources.label: studio-interns.com — Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop ⌘U
sources.evidence: The page title gives the command as ⌘U: set locators by the selected regions, events or marquee and enable Cycle, with no rounding.

sources.label: afteraudio.com — Key commands for Global Commands in Logic Pro
sources.evidence: A copy of the Global Commands key command table. It came up for the exact command name 'Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events and Enable Cycle'.

sources.label: Apple — Use the cycle area in Logic Pro (10.7-versioned page)
sources.evidence: The cycle area appears as a yellow strip in the ruler, and the left and right locators are its start and end points.

tricks.original_title: Toggle Catch to stop the screen running away
tricks.reason: Apple's current pages support the description of Catch and the Catch button in the menu bar. The default-key claim (backquote) is not settled: studio-interns says `, a search summary of shortcut references said ⌥O, and Apple gives no key. The key claim was removed. Apple's Catch settings that switch Catch back on automatically were added in its place.
tricks.final_title: Toggle Catch to stop the screen running away
tricks.final_body: With Catch on, the visible section of a window follows the playhead during playback. For detailed editing, click the Catch button in the Tracks area (or editor) menu bar to turn it off, and the view holds still. If it keeps switching back on, check Logic Pro > Settings > General > Catch: “Catch when starting playback” and “Catch when moving playhead” re-enable it.

sources.label: Apple — Control windows using Catch modes in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: In Catch mode the visible section of a window follows the playhead during playback or recording. Click the Catch button in the Tracks area (or editor) menu bar to turn it on. With it inactive, the display doesn't update even when the playhead moves past the window edge.

sources.label: Apple — Catch settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The Logic Pro > Settings > General > Catch pane has 'Catch when starting playback', which turns on Catch mode when you click Play or Pause, and 'Catch when moving playhead', which turns it on when you move the playhead.

tricks.original_title: Capture the last thing you played, even when not recording
tricks.reason: ⇧R, the Logic 11.2 audio requirement, focus, playing, incoming signal, the 4-second minimum and the 1-minute maximum are all confirmed. 'MIDI works on any recent version' is vague and has no source, so it was removed. The MIDI page confirms capture works whether the project is playing or stopped. Wording now follows Apple's.
tricks.final_title: Capture the last thing you played, even when not recording
tricks.final_body: If you played something great without recording, press ⇧R (Flashback Capture) and Logic turns it into a region. MIDI can be captured whether the project is playing or stopped. Audio capture arrived in Logic 11.2: give the audio track focus and play the project. Logic saves audio only while there is an incoming signal, needs at least four seconds of playback, and keeps up to one minute.

sources.label: Apple — Capture a recent audio performance in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Click an audio track to give it focus and play; with the track in focus, click Flashback Capture or press Shift-R. Audio is captured only while the project is playing and there is an incoming signal. The project must play at least four seconds, and up to one minute of audio can be saved.

sources.label: Apple — Capture your most recent MIDI performance in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: You can capture MIDI notes while a project is playing or stopped. With a software instrument track focused, click Flashback Capture or press Shift-R.

sources.label: Apple — What's new in Logic Pro for Mac 11.2
sources.evidence: Apple's 11.2 what's-new page. Search results describe 11.2 as the release that brought Flashback Capture to audio.

sources.label: Logic Studio Training — Logic Pro 11.2 Update: Flashback Recording
sources.evidence: Says Flashback Capture captures audio on the focused track whenever the project is playing and an audio signal is present, new in 11.2.

tricks.original_title: Use the Step Input Keyboard for parts you cannot play
tricks.reason: Not rewritten. The prior audit's current Apple page confirms the menu path Window > Show Step Input Keyboard and entering one note at a time with chosen length and velocity. Search budget went to the rewritten tricks.
tricks.final_title: Use the Step Input Keyboard for parts you cannot play
tricks.final_body: Window > Show Step Input Keyboard. Enter notes one at a time at an exact rhythmic value. Complex parts get entered accurately without a single quantise pass.

sources.label: Apple — Use step input recording techniques in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Choose Window > Show Step Input Keyboard; click a key to insert a note, and use the Note Length and Velocity buttons to set its length and velocity (quote from the prior audit).

tricks.original_title: Draw notes with the Pencil, delete with the Eraser
tricks.reason: Every claim checks out on current Apple pages. A new note takes the length, velocity and channel of the note you last created or edited. You delete notes by selecting them and pressing Delete, or with the Eraser. Option-dragging copies notes.
tricks.final_title: Draw notes with the Pencil, delete with the Eraser
tricks.final_body: The Pencil creates a note whose length, velocity and MIDI channel match the last note you created or edited. To remove a note, select it and press Delete, or click it with the Eraser tool. ⌥-drag a note to copy it to a new position.

sources.label: Apple — Add notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Select the Pencil tool and click the background to create a note. The new note's length, velocity and channel match the previously created or edited note.

sources.label: Apple — Delete notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Delete notes by selecting them and pressing Delete, or with the Eraser tool (quote from the prior audit).

sources.label: Apple — Copy notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: You can Option-drag notes to a new position to copy them.

tricks.original_title: Use the Chord Trigger MIDI plugin to play chords with one finger
tricks.reason: The rewritten order is confirmed by the current Apple page: click Learn, click the trigger key on the upper keyboard, click the chord notes on the lower keyboard, then click Learn to end.
tricks.final_title: Use the Chord Trigger MIDI plugin to play chords with one finger
tricks.final_body: Insert Chord Trigger in the MIDI FX slot and click Learn. Click the trigger key you want on the upper keyboard first, then click the notes of the chord on the lower keyboard, then click Learn again to finish. Whole progressions become one-finger performances.

sources.label: Apple — Use Chord Trigger in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Click Learn (the label changes to Trigger Key), click a trigger key on the upper keyboard (the label changes to Chord), click the notes on the lower keyboard, then click Learn to end chord assignment.

sources.label: Apple — Chord Trigger overview in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Apple's overview page for the Chord Trigger MIDI plug-in.

tricks.original_title: Force everything into key with Transposer's scale quantize
tricks.reason: The title still names a 'scale quantize' control that doesn't exist. Apple's mechanism is the Root and Scale menus. 'Pulled to the nearest right one' appeared only in a search-engine summary, not in Apple's text, so it was replaced with Apple's wording: notes are corrected to the selected scale. The User scale and on-screen keyboard claim is confirmed.
tricks.final_title: Force everything into key with Transposer
tricks.final_body: Insert the Transposer MIDI FX and set its Root and Scale pop-up menus. Transposer transposes incoming MIDI notes in real time and corrects them to the selected scale, so you stay in key as you play. Choose User and click notes off on the on-screen keyboard to build your own scale.

sources.label: Apple — Transposer in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Transposer can transpose incoming MIDI notes in real time and correct notes to a selected scale. Root pop-up: choose the root note. Scale pop-up: presets or a custom User scale. Keyboard: click notes on or off; notes turned off are excluded from the User scale.

tricks.original_title: Use Arpeggiator to generate parts, then commit them
tricks.reason: The current Apple page confirms the Bounce in Place facts: selected regions rendered with all active plug-ins and automation data to 24-bit audio at the project sample rate. Only the wording changed ('every active plug-in and its automation' became Apple's 'all active plug-ins and automation data').
tricks.final_title: Use Arpeggiator to generate parts, then commit them
tricks.final_body: Insert Arpeggiator and dial in a pattern, then commit it with Bounce in Place. Logic renders the selected region, including all active plug-ins and automation data, to a 24-bit audio file at the project sample rate. The live pattern becomes a fixed part you can edit as audio.

sources.label: Apple — Logic Pro for Mac bounce in place overview
sources.evidence: You can render one or more selected regions on audio or software instrument tracks, including all active plug-ins and automation data. The bounce is 24-bit at the project sample rate.

sources.label: Apple — Bounce regions in place in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Apple's current how-to page for Bounce in Place on regions.

tricks.original_title: Transpose without touching the notes
tricks.reason: The Transpose parameter's playback-only behavior is confirmed. 'Audition a key change for the whole song' overreaches: it acts only on the MIDI regions you select, and audio regions are not covered. The text now limits itself to MIDI regions. The Apple region-parameters page found is /10.7/, so macProVideo is cited as an independent second source, alongside the current Region inspector page.
tricks.final_title: Transpose without touching the notes
tricks.final_body: Select MIDI regions and set the Region inspector's Transpose field. The notes are transposed in semitones during playback while the recorded notes stay as they are, so you can try a new key and back out in seconds.

sources.label: Apple — Logic Pro MIDI region parameters
sources.evidence: Transpose: all note events in the region are transposed up or down in semitones during playback.

sources.label: Apple — Use the Region inspector in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Current page: the Region inspector shows parameters for the selected region or regions.

sources.label: macProVideo — Real-Time MIDI Editing In Logic Pro X
sources.evidence: Search summary: region parameter settings, including transposition, are applied in real time during playback.

tricks.original_title: Use the Modifier MIDI plugin to remap anything to anything
tricks.reason: Input Event, Re-Assign To, Scale (scaling) and Add (offset) are all confirmed on the current Apple page. The examples 'modwheel into aftertouch, pitchbend into expression' were not confirmed by any retrieved source, so they were removed. The title's 'anything to anything' contradicts Apple's single-controller scope.
tricks.final_title: Use the Modifier MIDI plugin to reassign a controller
tricks.final_body: The Modifier MIDI plug-in reassigns or filters a single continuous controller or fader event. Choose or learn the incoming type in Input Event and the outgoing type in Re-Assign To, then use the Scale and Add sliders to scale or offset the output values.

sources.label: Apple — Modifier in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Modifier lets you reassign or filter a single continuous controller or fader event and scale or add to its values. Input Event and Re-Assign To choose or learn the input and output event types. Scale sets the scaling amount and Add sets the offset for the output event.

tricks.original_title: Merge takes when you are layering, not replacing
tricks.reason: Not rewritten. The prior audit's current Apple Recording settings page describes Merge exactly as the trick does. Search budget went to the rewritten tricks.
tricks.final_title: Merge takes when you are layering, not replacing
tricks.final_body: For building up a drum pattern one element per pass, set MIDI cycle recording to Merge instead. Each loop adds to the same region.

sources.label: Apple — Recording settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Merge merges the MIDI recorded in each cycle pass with the previously recorded MIDI of overlapping regions into a single MIDI region (quote from the prior audit).

tricks.original_title: Freeze the instrument as soon as the part is done
tricks.reason: Apple's only pages describing the Freeze button 'in the track header' were /10.7/ pages, so the button location isn't supported for Logic 11/12 and was dropped. The current Bounce in Place overview confirms that Freeze saves CPU by rendering the track's instrument and effect plug-ins, and that it is easier to reverse than Bounce in Place.
tricks.final_title: Freeze the instrument as soon as the part is done
tricks.final_body: Freeze the software instrument track once the part is done. Logic renders its instrument and effect plug-ins so they stop costing CPU, and unlike Bounce in Place, Freeze lets you return to the original track and its automation more easily.

sources.label: Apple — Logic Pro for Mac bounce in place overview
sources.evidence: Both Bounce in Place and Freeze save CPU power by rendering all effect and instrument plug-ins of a track. However, Freeze allows you to return to the original state of the tracks and their automation data more easily.

sources.label: Apple — Freeze tracks in Logic Pro (10.7 guide, supporting only)
sources.evidence: Freezing bounces the track to an audio file that includes plug-in output and automation, and reduces the processing power needed. Cited for the mechanism only, not for UI names.

tricks.original_title: Drag a MIDI region onto an audio track to bounce it instantly
tricks.reason: No source supports the title's gesture (dragging a MIDI region onto an audio track). The body, which describes Bounce in Place, is confirmed by the current Apple page, so the title now matches the body. 'It is the fastest way' is an unsupported superlative and was removed. The trick now overlaps trick 5; the editor may want to merge them.
tricks.final_title: Commit a MIDI region to audio with Bounce in Place
tricks.final_body: Select the MIDI region and use Bounce in Place. Logic renders it through the instrument and all active plug-ins, plus automation data, to a 24-bit audio region at the project sample rate, which locks the idea in as audio.

sources.label: Apple — Logic Pro for Mac bounce in place overview
sources.evidence: Render selected regions on audio or software instrument tracks, including all active plug-ins and automation data. The bounce is 24-bit at the project sample rate.

sources.label: Apple — Bounce regions in place in Logic Pro for Mac

tricks.original_title: Keep one “sketch” instrument track loaded at all times
tricks.reason: A pure workflow habit. It makes no checkable claim about how a Logic feature behaves.
tricks.final_title: Keep one “sketch” instrument track loaded at all times
tricks.final_body: A piano patch on a permanently armed track means any idea is three seconds from being captured. The moment capture takes effort, ideas stop arriving.

tricks.original_title: Use Note Repeat for hi‑hats and rolls
tricks.reason: Confirmed on current Apple pages: Note Repeat is chosen from the Edit Mode selector, you drag up or down on a step to change the number of slices (1 to 16), and the inspector has Velocity Ramp, Velocity Curve and Distribution per step. Distribution produces the accelerando or decelerando.
tricks.final_title: Use Note Repeat for hi‑hats and rolls
tricks.final_body: In Step Sequencer, choose Note Repeat from the Edit Mode selector, then drag up on a hi-hat step to slice it into more repeats (1 to 16) or down for fewer. The inspector adds velocity ramp, velocity curve and Distribution for each step, so a roll can accelerate or decelerate instead of sitting flat.

sources.label: Apple — Use Step Sequencer edit modes in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Select Note Repeat from the Edit Mode selector and drag up on a step to increase slices or down to decrease them; values range from 1 to 16. The inspector sets velocity ramp, velocity curve and distribution per step, and Distribution creates accelerando or decelerando.

sources.label: Apple — Edit Step Sequencer pattern, row, and step settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Apple's current page for the Step Sequencer inspector settings.

tricks.original_title: Force legato to fix gappy pads
tricks.reason: 9to5Mac and Your Local Musician both give the exact path Edit > Trim > Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato) and say notes extend to end where the next note begins. A Logic Pro Help forum thread uses the same command name. Apple's current Resize notes page confirms the Edit > Trim submenu in the Piano Roll menu bar holds these length commands.
tricks.final_title: Force legato to fix gappy pads
tricks.final_body: Select the notes, then choose Edit > Trim > Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato) in the Piano Roll. Every note extends to end where the next one begins, and pads and basslines stop sounding stuttery instantly.

sources.label: 9to5Mac — The Logic Pros: 3 helpful tricks to streamline your MIDI/audio editing
sources.evidence: Highlight the notes in the piano roll and click Edit > Trim > Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato); the MIDI extends to end where the next note begins.

sources.evidence: Force Legato lengthens each note so it ends at the start of the following note.

sources.label: Apple — Resize notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: The Edit > Trim submenu in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar has commands that change the length of selected notes relative to the notes around them.

tricks.original_title: Trim overlaps automatically
tricks.reason: Apple's current Resize notes page confirms 'Note End to Remove Overlaps to Following Notes (8 Ticks Gap)' with the eight-tick gap, plus a 'Selected Notes' version. Two claims were removed: 'stops the phasing and stuck voices you get on hardware' (no source) and the 'repeated notes' version (not confirmed this session).
tricks.final_title: Trim overlaps automatically
tricks.final_body: Select the notes and choose Edit > Trim > Note End to Remove Overlaps to Following Notes (8 Ticks Gap) in the Piano Roll. Logic shortens the note ends so nothing overlaps, leaving an eight-tick gap before the next note. A Selected Notes version does the same job measured only against the other selected notes.

sources.label: Apple — Resize notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: 'Note End to Remove Overlaps to Following Notes (8 Ticks Gap)' trims selected note ends so none overlap adjacent notes, leaving an eight-tick gap. 'Note End to Remove Overlaps to Selected Notes (8 Ticks Gap)' leaves an eight-tick gap before the next selected note.

tricks.original_title: ⌥‑drag a note to duplicate it
tricks.reason: Apple's current Copy notes page confirms Option-drag to copy, including between two Piano Roll Editor windows and between the Piano Roll windows of different projects. Apple's current Move notes page confirms the setting path and name, that the first drag direction limits movement, and that Shift while dragging switches between the two behaviours.
tricks.final_title: ⌥‑drag a note to duplicate it
tricks.final_body: Hold ⌥ while dragging any note or selection to copy rather than move — you can even ⌥-drag notes between two Piano Roll windows, or between two different projects. To stop a drag changing pitch, turn on Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing > "Limit Dragging to One Direction In Piano Roll and Score": the direction you start in is then the only one you can move in. Pressing ⇧ while dragging switches that behaviour on and off; it is not a pitch lock on its own.

sources.label: Apple — Copy notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Option-drag notes to a new position to copy them. You can Option-drag between two Piano Roll Editor windows, or between the Piano Roll Editor windows of different projects.

sources.label: Apple — Move notes in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Choose Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing and select 'Limit Dragging to One Direction In Piano Roll and Score'. The first direction restricts movement to that plane, and Shift while dragging switches between the two behaviours.

tricks.original_title: Place a note between grid divisions
tricks.reason: Apple's current Snap page confirms Ticks = 1/3840 of a beat, and Apple's current Move notes page confirms Control-Shift drag moves in tick steps and overrides Snap. The ⌃⌥ Zoom-tool warning was removed because no source for it was retrieved this session. The Snap page also documents an On/Off button beside the Snap pop-up menu, so that option was added.
tricks.final_title: Place a note between grid divisions
tricks.final_body: Set the Snap pop-up menu to Ticks, which snaps to 1/3840 of a beat, or press Control-Shift as you drag to move the note in tick steps, overriding the Snap value. You can also switch snapping off with the On/Off button beside the Snap pop-up menu.

tricks.original_title: Change velocity by dragging with the Velocity tool
tricks.reason: Apple's current Edit velocity page confirms the Velocity tool from the Tool menu, Control-Command for temporary access, the help tag that updates as you drag, and View > Set Note Color > By Velocity (warm = high, cool = low). The sentence about the line inside the note was dropped because it was not re-confirmed this session.
tricks.final_title: Change velocity by dragging with the Velocity tool
tricks.final_body: Pick the Velocity tool from the Tool menu, or hold Control-Command to turn the Pointer into it temporarily, then drag up or down on a note. A help tag shows the velocity as you drag. Choose View > Set Note Color > By Velocity if you want the note colour to track it too.

sources.label: Apple — Edit velocity in the Piano Roll Editor in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Drag vertically over a note with the Velocity tool, chosen from the Tool menu or reached by pressing Control-Command. A help tag shows the velocity as you drag. View > Set Note Color > By Velocity shows velocity as colour.

tricks.original_title: Show the automation lane inside the Piano Roll
tricks.reason: Apple's current Automation/MIDI area page confirms the Show/Hide Automation button in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar, the Automation/MIDI Parameter pop-up menu, and that data for the chosen parameter shows in the Automation/MIDI lane under the main editor. tricks.final_title: Show the automation lane inside the Piano Roll
tricks.final_body: Click the Show/Hide Automation button in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar, then choose a parameter from the Automation/MIDI Parameter pop-up menu. Its MIDI or automation data appears in a lane under the notes, where you can edit it. Track automation shown there is the same curve as in the Tracks area, so edits appear in both places.

tricks.final_title: Colour notes by velocity to read dynamics instantly
tricks.final_body: In the Piano Roll's View menu, set note colour to Velocity. Flat parts become visibly, obviously flat.

tricks.final_title: Quantise from the region inspector, not destructively
tricks.final_body: The Quantize field in the Region inspector is non‑destructive and can be dialled back or removed at any point. Use it before you ever use the destructive version.

tricks.original_title: Check your input with the channel strip's meter, not your ears
tricks.reason: SOS supports the -12 dBFS peak target and says recording hot won't improve actual noise performance and makes mixing harder. It does not say hot recording 'buys you nothing' (SOS names S/N as the only possible advantage), and 'a habit from tape' was not checked. Reworded to match SOS.
tricks.final_title: Check your input with the channel strip's meter, not your ears
tricks.final_body: Aim for peaks around −12 dBFS with your loudest phrase. In 24-bit, recording hot won't improve the real-world noise performance. It just makes the track harder to mix against others recorded with sensible headroom.

sources.label: Sound On Sound — Q. How much headroom should I leave with 24-bit recording?
sources.evidence: Set the highest peaks between -12 and -18 dBFS; recording 'hot' won't improve actual noise performance and makes it harder to mix against tracks recorded with more headroom.

sources.label: Sound On Sound — Q. Should I gain-stage to -6dBFS or -18dBFS?
sources.evidence: Returned in the same search. SOS guidance on 24-bit headroom is average around -18/-20 dBFS with peaks around -10 dBFS.

tricks.original_title: Drop the buffer to 64 samples for tracking
tricks.reason: Apple supports: use the lowest buffer setting when recording, raise it one step on system overload alerts, and read the round-trip latency shown under the I/O Buffer Size menu (Settings > Audio > Devices). No source supports '64 samples', so it was removed from the title. The vague 'Audio settings' is now the documented path.
tricks.final_title: Drop the I/O buffer to its lowest setting for tracking
tricks.final_body: Set the buffer before tracking, not during. In Logic Pro > Settings > Audio > Devices, choose the lowest I/O Buffer Size your Mac can handle. If you get system overload alerts, step it up one setting. Logic shows the resulting round-trip latency under the I/O Buffer Size menu, so judge by that readout, not the sample number.

sources.label: Apple — Manage input monitoring latency in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: When recording, set the buffer to the lowest setting; if you get system overload alerts, increase it to the next setting. Logic Pro > Settings > Audio > Devices > I/O Buffer Size; Logic shows the resulting latency under the I/O Buffer Size menu.

tricks.original_title: Turn on Low Latency Mode instead of disabling plugins one by one
tricks.reason: Apple supports the Limit slider in Settings > Audio > General (up to 30 ms), bypassing plug-ins that exceed the latency value, Aux sends being turned off, and the scope (the focused instrument track plus Input Monitoring or Record Enable tracks). 'Quiet chains sound identical' is not documented, so it was removed. The title now uses Apple's name for the mode.
tricks.final_title: Turn on Low Latency Monitoring mode instead of disabling plug-ins one by one
tricks.final_body: Low Latency Monitoring mode bypasses the latency-inducing plug-ins that push a track past the Limit slider in Logic Pro > Settings > Audio > General (up to 30 ms). It also turns off that track's Aux sends, which kills a headphone reverb fed from a send. It affects only the focused instrument track and tracks with Input Monitoring or Record Enable on.

sources.label: Apple — Work with plug-in latencies in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Logic Pro automatically bypasses latency-inducing plug-ins that exceed a specific latency value and turns off any Aux sends on that track; the Limit slider in Settings > Audio > General sets the maximum allowed latency (up to 30 ms); the mode affects only the focused instrument track and tracks with Input Monitoring or Record Enable active.

tricks.original_title: Count-in and pre-roll are either/or — pick the right one
tricks.reason: Apple's Recording project settings confirm the When Beginning choice between count-in (bars or beats) and pre-roll (playback time up to 60 seconds). The claim that count-in 'stays locked to the tempo map' is not in the source, so it was removed. The rest is usage advice built on those units.
tricks.final_title: Count-in and pre-roll are either/or — pick the right one
tricks.final_body: In the Recording project settings, the When Beginning buttons make you choose a count-in or a pre-roll. Count-in is set in bars or beats. Pre-roll is a playback time in seconds, up to 60. Use pre-roll when bars mean nothing (free-tempo material, dialogue) and count-in when you want the performer counted in musically.

sources.label: Apple — Recording project settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: When Beginning buttons choose between a count-in or pre-roll; Count-in selects a number of bars or beats; the Pre-roll slider sets the playback time (up to 60 seconds) before recording starts.

tricks.reason: Search budget ran out, so this relies on the prior audit's current Apple page, which confirms that regions and their source audio files take the track name. The exact 'Audio 3#12.wav' filename format was never checked, so the example is now a generic default name.
tricks.final_title: Name the track before you record, always
tricks.final_body: Logic names recorded regions and their audio files after the track. A default name like “Audio 3” means nothing to you three months later.

sources.label: Apple — Rename tracks in Logic Pro for Mac (from prior audit; not re-retrieved this session)

tricks.original_title: Record‑enable multiple tracks at once
tricks.reason: Every claim matches Apple's current page: clicking each Record Enable button makes it blink red; Option-click makes that track the only record-ready track; Option-clicking a blinking button makes all tracks not record-ready.
tricks.final_title: Record‑enable multiple tracks at once
tricks.final_body: Record‑enable multiple tracks at once. Click the Record Enable button in the track header of each track you want to record to — every armed button blinks red. Option-click is the escape hatch, not the shortcut: Option-clicking a track's Record Enable button makes it the only record-ready track, and Option-clicking a track that is already blinking red clears record-ready status across the whole project. Learn it as "solo the arm" and "disarm everything", and you will never lose a multitrack take to a stray modifier.

sources.label: Apple — Record to multiple audio tracks in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Click the Record Enable button of each track; each blinks red. Option-click a track's Record Enable button to make it the only record-ready track; Option-click any track whose button is blinking red to make all record-ready tracks not record-ready.

tricks.final_title: Watch the take list, not the waveform
tricks.final_body: The Take Folder pop-up menu in the upper-left corner of a take folder lists every take you've banked, and you can pick one from it during playback. If the performer is on take 14 and getting worse, that list is your cue to stop and move on.

tricks.final_title: Build a dedicated headphone mix on a bus
tricks.final_body: Send every track to a second output bus and give the performer more of themselves and more reverb than you would ever put in the mix. Comfort produces better takes than accuracy does.

tricks.final_title: Use Input Monitoring rather than record enable to rehearse
tricks.final_body: The Input Monitoring (I) button in the track header lets you hear a track that isn't record-enabled, so you can set levels and practise the part before committing. On audio tracks it still involves some latency, depending on your hardware and driver settings.

sources.label: Apple — Use input monitoring with tracks in Logic Pro for Mac

tricks.original_title: Turn off software monitoring if you hear yourself twice
tricks.reason: Apple says software monitoring always adds some delay, and says to turn it off when your interface supports hardware monitoring. It can also be toggled from a control bar button. tricks.final_title: Turn off software monitoring if you hear yourself twice
tricks.final_body: If your interface's hardware monitoring is on, you're also hearing Logic's software-monitored copy, which always carries some delay. Pick one. Apple's advice when your interface supports hardware monitoring: turn off Software monitoring in Logic Pro > Settings > Audio > General, or with its control bar button.

sources.label: Apple — General Audio settings in Logic Pro for Mac
sources.evidence: Software monitoring checkbox: with it on, audio is processed via software and some latency is inevitable; if you listen through your mixing console or your interface supports hardware monitoring, turn it off. It can also be toggled with a Software Monitoring button in the control bar.
